description:
We are an established team focused on analyzing Earth-based geological analogs for lunar and Martian human habitats. Our team utilizes GIS mapping, planetary data analysis, and interactive UI design to assess potential base locations.

Note: Our team membership is currently complete and full.
summary: AethelGeo Analogue Explorer is an interactive web platform and 3D model which helps you to find places on Earth that could act as analogues for candidate Moon and Mars sites. We're looking at some of the less well known areas in Azerbaijan (Dashkasan, Goygol and Gobustan) and comparing them to the lunar and martian target areas using a number of terrain based measures: slope distribution, relief and surface roughness, plus some rover relevant traversability. A Python pipeline takes those measures along with the literature based geology descriptors and produces an Analog Match Score across 5 categories (Terrain, Geology, Environment, Resources and Operations). Any missing data is never scored as zero, it is simply omitted and the result is marked' Incomplete'. All values have a reliability label (Measured, Literature, Unverified or Demo). For each pair you can see exactly where the analogy works and where it doesn't and there is a Blender built 3d view which allows you to compare the terrains side by side in terms of elevation, slope and roughness. It's obviously a lot cheaper and safer to test your equipment and operations on Earth prior to going to the Moon and Mars, but only if you actually know how good the analogy is and where it breaks down.
details:
AethelGeo Analogue Explorer enables you to compare candidate Moon and Mars sites with terrestrial locations to see which Earth sites could act as analogues and where the analogy breaks down.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The platform compares the candidate sites in Azerbaijan (Dashkasan, Goygol and Gobustan) with the candidate lunar and Martian regions. A Python pipeline takes the DEMS and calculates a range of terrain metrics including slope distribution, relief and slope variability, and the proportion of the area that a rover could traverse. It also has a range of literature based geology descriptors. From this it produces an Analog Match Score from 0 to 100 across five categories (Terrain, Geology, Environment, Resources and Operations). A category with no data is simply left out and the result is marked Incomplete (not scored as zero). Each value has a reliability tag (Measured, Literature, Unverified or Demo) and there is a sensitivity check to see whether the site ranking changes if the weights are changed. A Blender script then creates a 3D view of the Earth, Moon and Mars terrain blocks with the colouring based on elevation, slope and roughness, which are then exported as GLB files for the web.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Researchers, mission planners and students can compare sites on the basis of quantifiable characteristics and assess the reliability of each number rather than just relying on visual similarity. The technique can be applied to other sites by simply incorporating new elevation data.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, pandas, rasterio, matplotlib), Google collab, Blender and its Python API, GLB and a web front end (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) all hosted on Netlify.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

We're looking at measurable attributes rather than appearance. Missing data is dealt with transparently, observed values are distinguished from published hypotheses and we show where any analogy fails. We've looked at the various resolutions of the Earth, Moon and Mars elevation data and the limits of any Earth analogue (Earth can't replicate the reduced gravity, the lunar vacuum, the thin Martian atmosphere or the radiation). A high score simply indicates similarity on the chosen measurements, it doesn't prove the existence of an analogue.

The current results in this version are prototype outputs and are tagged with a reliability rating on the site.
